title: Fever in Children Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing fever in children, identifying serious infections, age-specific risks, and distinguishing viral from bacterial causes.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, sepsis protocols or urgent escalation.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Meningitis (fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash, altered consciousness)
Bacteraemia or serious bacterial infection (high fever, unwell appearance, risk factors)
Sepsis (fever with signs of shock: pallor, poor perfusion, lethargy)
Urinary tract infection (fever <3yrs with no source, dysuria if older)
Epiglottitis or severe airway infection (stridor, drooling, difficulty swallowing)
Febrile convulsion (seizure during high fever; exclude other CNS causes)
Immunosuppression or significant comorbidity increasing risk
items.importantLimitation: Serious bacterial infection can present with fever alone. Absence of focal signs does not exclude serious infection in young children.

items.title: Age and fever height
mustConfirmOrExclude: Age (<3 months, 3-36 months, >36 months risk stratification)
Fever height and duration
Vaccination status (Hib, pneumococcal)
Preceding illness or sick contacts
Recent antibiotics

items.title: Red flags
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever with non-blanching rash
Fever with lethargy or difficulty arousing
Fever with breathing difficulty or stridor
Fever with inability to drink or signs of dehydration
Fever with severe abdominal or joint pain
History of febrile convulsions

items.title: Meningitis
urgentFeatures: Fever with neck stiffness, petechial/purpuric rash, altered consciousness
Fever with signs of severe systemic illness

items.title: Urinary tract infection
urgentFeatures: Fever <3 years with no obvious source (most common serious bacterial infection)
Dysuria, frequency, abdominal/flank pain if older
Nitrites or leucocytes on urine dipstick
implications: Urine culture and antibiotics; imaging assessment

items.title: Serious bacterial infection
urgentFeatures: High fever (>39°C) with unwell appearance in unvaccinated or partially vaccinated child
Toxic appearance: lethargy, poor perfusion, mottled skin
Signs of focal infection (chest, abdomen, ENT) with severe fever
implications: Blood cultures; antibiotics and hospital referral

items.title: General appearance
howToTest: Level of consciousness: alert, drowsy, unrousable?
Presence of rash: blanching, non-blanching, petechial?
normal: Alert and interactive, normal colour, warm peripheries, no rash
abnormal: Lethargy, drowsiness, mottled/pale, poor perfusion, petechial or non-blanching rash
implications: Abnormal appearance suggests serious infection or sepsis

items.title: Meningeal signs
howToTest: Kernig and Brudzinski signs (if old enough)
normal: No neck stiffness, no bulging fontanelle
abnormal: Neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle, positive Kernig/Brudzinski
implications: Meningeal signs require emergency referral and empiric antibiotics

items.title: Viral infection
commonFindings: Fever with URI symptoms: runny nose, cough, sore throat
implications: Supportive care; no antibiotics for viral illness

items.title: Roseola infantum
commonFindings: High fever in infants 6-24 months lasting 3-4 days
Rose-pink maculopapular rash after fever defervesces

items.title: Scarlet fever
commonFindings: Fever with sore throat and fine scarlatiniform rash

items.title: Fever with no obvious source
commonFindings: Fever in child <3 years with no localising signs
UTI most common serious bacterial cause
implications: Urine culture mandatory; consider blood culture if toxic appearance

items.title: Investigation approach (age-dependent)
mustConfirmOrExclude: <3 months: low threshold for hospitalisation and full septic workup
3-36 months: assess risk; urine culture always; blood culture if toxic
Lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected (after imaging if focal signs)

items.title: Home management when
mustConfirmOrExclude: Low-risk appearance and vital signs
Non-blanching rash absent
Can maintain fluids
Reliable follow-up available

items.title: Urgent hospital referral
urgentFeatures: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever
Signs of shock or severe systemic illness
Unvaccinated or partially vaccinated child with high fever and toxic appearance

items.title: Fever in children
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: non-blanching rash with fever; lethargy or difficulty arousing; difficulty breathing or stridor; fever <3 months of age; or signs of shock (pale, mottled, poor perfusion)

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: fever >39°C with unwell appearance; fever with neck stiffness or bulging fontanelle; fever with severe abdominal or joint pain; fever with inability to drink; or fever lasting >5 days with no clear source
Speak to your GP if: fever is resolving but you want follow-up; child has recurrent fevers; or you want guidance on paracetamol/ibuprofen dosing
